about: Mechanical Vibrations is a Part IA course in the Cambridge Engineering Tripos; in 2025-26 it was given as 12 lectures in weeks 7-8 of Lent Term and weeks 1-4 of Easter Term. Following the official syllabus, it builds equations of motion from masses, springs and dashpots (with their electrical analogues), solves first- and second-order systems for step, ramp, impulse and harmonic inputs, introduces damping measures, and extends to systems with two or more degrees of freedom, including mode shapes, vibration isolation and absorbers. It is examined in Part IA Paper 1 (Mechanical Engineering), a 3-hour paper (per the 2025-26 Part IA guide) shared with Mechanics and Thermofluid Mechanics. Topics and order follow the 2025-26 course page; check the 2026-27 page and Moodle for any changes.

notes.h: System elements, analogues and equations of motion
notes.body:
The course starts by building every vibrating system from a few ideal elements and writing down its differential equation. Getting this step right is half of most exam questions.

The ideal elements (translational)
- Mass m: force needed = mẍ. Stores kinetic energy ½mẋ².
- Linear spring of stiffness k: force = k × (extension). Stores strain energy ½kx².
- Viscous dashpot of coefficient c: force = c × (relative velocity of its ends). Dissipates energy.
- Rotational versions: a rotor with moment of inertia J (torque Jθ̈), a torsional spring k_t (torque k_tθ) and a rotary damper c_t (torque c_tθ̇).

Combining springs
- Springs in parallel (same displacement) add: k = k₁ + k₂.
- Springs in series (same force) add as reciprocals: 1/k = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂. Two springs 2k and 3k in series give 6k/5.

Electrical analogues
- A series inductor–resistor–capacitor circuit driven by voltage V obeys Lq̈ + Rq̇ + q/C = V, where q is charge.
- Compare mẍ + cẋ + kx = F: mass ↔ inductance L, dashpot ↔ resistance R, spring stiffness ↔ 1/C (spring compliance ↔ capacitance), displacement ↔ charge, force ↔ voltage.
- So the natural frequency 1/√(LC) and damping of a tuned circuit behave exactly like √(k/m) and the damping of a mass–spring–dashpot. This is why the same mathematics appears in 1P3.

Writing equations of motion
- Choose coordinates (one per degree of freedom) and measure them from static equilibrium. For a mass hanging on a spring, gravity is then balanced by the static spring extension and drops out of the equation.
- Displace each coordinate a little in the positive direction and draw a free-body diagram of each mass, showing spring and dashpot forces in terms of the relative displacements and velocities of their ends.
- Apply Newton's second law (or moments for a rotor).
- Single-degree-of-freedom result: mẍ + cẋ + kx = F(t).
- If the input is a displacement y(t) of the base through a spring and dashpot: mẍ + c(ẋ − ẏ) + k(x − y) = 0, i.e. mẍ + cẋ + kx = cẏ + ky.

Standard forms
- First order (no mass): Tẏ + y = x(t), with time constant T. A spring k in parallel with a dashpot c pushed by force F gives cẋ + kx = F, so T = c/k. An RC circuit gives T = RC.
- Second order: divide mẍ + cẋ + kx = F by k to get (1/ωn²)ẍ + (2ζ/ωn)ẋ + x = F/k, with ωn = √(k/m) and ζ = c/(2√(km)). The right-hand side is the static deflection the force would cause.

Exam tips: always state where each coordinate is measured from and check signs by imagining one mass displaced while the others are held still.

notes.h: First-order systems: step, ramp and impulse response
notes.body:
First-order systems have no inertia, or one storage element only. They do not oscillate; they relax towards equilibrium with a single time constant.

Standard form
- Tẏ + y = x(t), where x is the input, y the output and T the time constant.
- Mechanical example: a spring k in parallel with a dashpot c, loaded by force F: cẏ + ky = F, so T = c/k with input F/k.
- Electrical example: an RC circuit, with T = RC.

Unit step response (x jumps from 0 to 1 at t = 0, y(0) = 0)
- y = 1 − e^(−t/T).
- At t = T the output has reached 1 − e⁻¹ ≈ 63.2% of its final value. The initial slope is 1/T, so a tangent drawn at t = 0 reaches the final value at t = T.
- After 3T it is within 5%; after 5T within about 0.7%.
- Example: c = 50 N s/m and k = 1000 N/m give T = 0.05 s, so the response reaches 95% at t = T ln 20 ≈ 0.15 s.

Unit ramp response (x = t, y(0) = 0)
- y = t − T + T e^(−t/T).
- After the transient dies away, the output follows the ramp with the same slope but lags it by T in time (an error of T in magnitude).

Unit impulse response (x = δ(t))
- y = (1/T) e^(−t/T).
- An impulse instantly sets y to 1/T, which then decays.

How the responses are linked
- The unit impulse is the derivative of the unit step, which is the derivative of the unit ramp. For a linear system the responses are linked in the same way: the impulse response is the time derivative of the step response, and the step response is the derivative of the ramp response.
- Check: d/dt(t − T + Te^(−t/T)) = 1 − e^(−t/T), and d/dt(1 − e^(−t/T)) = (1/T)e^(−t/T).

Solving the equations
- The general solution is a particular integral (any solution that fits the input) plus the complementary function Ae^(−t/T), with A chosen to match the initial condition.
- Linearity means superposition works: a step of size 5 gives 5 times the unit step response, and a delayed input gives a delayed response.

Exam tips: sketch every response with its asymptote, mark t = T and 63%, and check your answer at t = 0 and as t → ∞.

notes.h: Harmonic response and the exp(iωt) method
notes.body:
A linear system driven by a sinusoid settles into a sinusoidal response at the same frequency, with a different amplitude and a phase shift. Complex exponentials make this calculation almost mechanical.

The method
- Write the input as the real part of a complex exponential: x = X cos ωt = Re(X e^(iωt)).
- Look for a steady-state output y = Re(Y e^(iωt)), where Y is a complex amplitude.
- Differentiation becomes multiplication: d/dt → iω and d²/dt² → −ω².
- Substitute, cancel e^(iωt), and solve the resulting algebraic equation for Y/X, the frequency response (or transfer function).
- The amplitude ratio is |Y/X| and the phase of the output relative to the input is arg(Y/X). A negative argument means the output lags.
- Engineers in electrical work often write j instead of i; the mathematics is identical.

First-order example
- Tẏ + y = x gives (1 + iωT)Y = X, so Y/X = 1/(1 + iωT).
- Amplitude ratio |Y/X| = 1/√(1 + ω²T²). Phase lag φ = arctan(ωT).
- At low frequency (ωT ≪ 1) the output follows the input: ratio ≈ 1, lag ≈ 0.
- At ω = 1/T (the corner or break frequency), ratio = 1/√2 ≈ 0.707 (−3 dB) and the lag is 45°.
- At high frequency (ωT ≫ 1) the ratio ≈ 1/(ωT), falling by a factor of 10 for each tenfold rise in frequency, and the lag approaches 90°.
- Worked example: T = 0.01 s and ω = 200 rad/s give ωT = 2, ratio 1/√5 = 0.447 and lag arctan 2 = 63.4°.

Second-order preview
- mẍ + cẋ + kx = F₀ cos ωt gives X = F₀ / (k − mω² + icω). The same steps produce the resonance curves treated later.

Why it works
- For a linear system with constant coefficients, e^(iωt) is unchanged in form by differentiation, so the equation reduces to algebra. Taking the real part at the end is valid because the equation is linear with real coefficients.
- The complete solution is the steady-state harmonic response plus a transient (complementary function) that decays if the system is damped. "Harmonic response" in exam questions normally means the steady state.

Plotting frequency response
- Amplitude ratio and phase are usually plotted against frequency, often on logarithmic axes. These plots summarise how the system treats inputs at every frequency.

Exam tips: keep the complex algebra tidy by grouping real and imaginary parts in the denominator, find modulus and argument from that form, and check the low- and high-frequency limits make physical sense.

notes.h: Second-order systems: free vibration and damped SHM
notes.body:
A mass on a spring is the basic vibrating system. Adding a dashpot introduces damping, which controls how quickly the vibration dies away.

Undamped free vibration
- mẍ + kx = 0 has solution x = A cos ωn t + B sin ωn t, with natural frequency ωn = √(k/m) in rad/s (fn = ωn/2π in Hz).
- A and B come from the initial displacement x₀ and velocity v₀: A = x₀, B = v₀/ωn.
- This is simple harmonic motion: energy passes back and forth between kinetic and strain energy with constant total.

Damped free vibration
- mẍ + cẋ + kx = 0. Define the damping factor ζ = c/(2√(km)) = c/(2mωn). The critical damping coefficient is c_c = 2√(km), so ζ = c/c_c.
- Trying x = e^(λt) gives λ = −ζωn ± ωn√(ζ² − 1).
- Underdamped (ζ < 1): x = e^(−ζωn t)(A cos ωd t + B sin ωd t). The motion oscillates at the damped natural frequency ωd = ωn√(1 − ζ²) inside an exponentially decaying envelope. This is damped SHM.
- Critically damped (ζ = 1): x = (A + Bt)e^(−ωn t). It returns to rest fastest without overshooting.
- Overdamped (ζ > 1): the sum of two decaying exponentials; slow and sluggish, with no oscillation.
- Most engineering structures are lightly damped (ζ of a few per cent or less), so ωd is very close to ωn.

Worked example
- m = 2 kg, k = 800 N/m, c = 8 N s/m. Then ωn = √400 = 20 rad/s (3.18 Hz) and c_c = 2√(1600) = 80 N s/m, so ζ = 0.1.
- ωd = 20√(1 − 0.01) ≈ 19.9 rad/s: only about 0.5% below ωn.
- If released from rest at x₀: x = x₀ e^(−ζωn t)[cos ωd t + (ζ/√(1 − ζ²)) sin ωd t]. The envelope decays with time constant 1/(ζωn) = 0.5 s.

Rotational and electrical versions
- A rotor J on a torsional spring k_t: ωn = √(k_t/J).
- A series LCR circuit: ωn = 1/√(LC) and ζ = (R/2)√(C/L).

Energy view
- Damping removes energy every cycle. The envelope of an underdamped response falls by the same factor each cycle, which is the basis of the logarithmic decrement method for measuring ζ.

Exam tips: always compute ζ before deciding the form of the solution, give frequencies in rad/s unless asked for Hz, and remember that initial conditions fix the constants after you have chosen the form.

notes.h: Second-order systems: step and impulse response
notes.body:
Transient responses show how a structure or instrument reacts to sudden loads, and they reveal its damping.

Step response
- Apply a constant force F₀ suddenly at t = 0 to a system at rest: mẍ + cẋ + kx = F₀.
- Particular integral: the static deflection x_s = F₀/k.
- For ζ < 1, with x(0) = 0 and ẋ(0) = 0: x = x_s[1 − e^(−ζωn t)(cos ωd t + (ζ/√(1 − ζ²)) sin ωd t)].
- The response overshoots the static value and oscillates about it before settling.
- The first peak is at t = π/ωd, and the fractional overshoot is exp(−πζ/√(1 − ζ²)).
- Undamped limit (ζ = 0): x = x_s(1 − cos ωn t), so the peak is exactly 2x_s. A suddenly applied load gives twice the deflection of the same load applied slowly; this dynamic factor of 2 matters in design.
- Example: ζ = 0.1 gives an overshoot of exp(−0.316) ≈ 0.73, so the peak is about 1.73 times the static deflection.
- Critically damped and overdamped systems reach x_s without overshoot. Instruments are often designed with ζ around 0.6 to 0.7 as a compromise between speed and overshoot.

Impulse response
- An impulse I (a large force for a very short time) changes the momentum of the mass without moving it: immediately afterwards x = 0 and ẋ = I/m.
- The spring and dashpot give negligible impulse during the blow, so they can be ignored for that instant.
- Response for ζ < 1: x = (I/(mωd)) e^(−ζωn t) sin ωd t.
- Undamped: x = (I/(mωn)) sin ωn t, so the amplitude is the initial velocity divided by ωn.
- Example: m = 2 kg, k = 800 N/m, I = 4 N s gives v₀ = 2 m/s, ωn = 20 rad/s, and amplitude 0.1 m.

Ramp inputs
- For a ramp force, the steady response follows the ramp with a lag; the impulse, step and ramp responses are linked by differentiation just as for first-order systems.

General method
- Write the solution as particular integral + complementary function.
- Use the initial conditions on the complete solution, not just the complementary function. This is the most common source of lost marks.

Exam tips: sketch the step response with its overshoot and envelope, and check that x(0) and ẋ(0) are satisfied by your final expression.

notes.h: Second-order systems: harmonic response and resonance
notes.body:
Most machines produce periodic forces, so the steady response to a sinusoidal force is central to vibration engineering.

Complex method
- mẍ + cẋ + kx = F₀ cos ωt. Try x = Re(X e^(iωt)): (k − mω² + icω)X = F₀.
- In terms of the frequency ratio r = ω/ωn: X/(F₀/k) = 1/(1 − r² + 2iζr).
- Amplitude: |X|/(F₀/k) = 1/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²).
- Phase lag of displacement behind force: tan φ = 2ζr/(1 − r²), with φ between 0° and 180°.

Three regimes
- r ≪ 1 (stiffness-controlled): |X| ≈ F₀/k, response nearly in phase with the force. The structure behaves quasi-statically.
- r ≈ 1 (damping-controlled): at r = 1 the amplitude is (F₀/k)/(2ζ) = F₀/(cωn) and the lag is exactly 90°. Only damping limits the response.
- r ≫ 1 (mass-controlled): |X| ≈ F₀/(mω²), falling as 1/ω², and the displacement is nearly 180° out of phase with the force.
- For ζ < 1/√2 the amplitude peak is at r = √(1 − 2ζ²), slightly below ωn; for light damping it is effectively at ωn.

Worked example
- m = 2 kg, k = 800 N/m, c = 8 N s/m (ωn = 20 rad/s, ζ = 0.1), F₀ = 10 N.
- Static deflection F₀/k = 12.5 mm.
- At resonance: 12.5/(2 × 0.1) = 62.5 mm, five times the static value.
- At ω = 40 rad/s (r = 2): denominator √(9 + 0.16) = 3.03, so |X| ≈ 4.13 mm, lagging the force by about 172°.

Energy at resonance
- At r = 1 the velocity is in phase with the force, so the force does the most work per cycle; all of it is dissipated by the dashpot. This is why damping alone sets the resonant amplitude.

Velocity and acceleration
- Velocity amplitude = ω|X| and acceleration amplitude = ω²|X|. Accelerometers measure the latter.

Rotating unbalance
- A rotor with mass imbalance produces a force proportional to ω², so the force amplitude itself grows with speed. A machine running up to speed must pass through resonance, where the response can be large even if the force is smaller than at full speed.

Exam tips: always non-dimensionalise with r and ζ, sketch both amplitude and phase curves, and state which regime the operating point lies in before choosing a design change (stiffer, heavier or more damped).

notes.h: Damping factor, logarithmic decrement and loss factor
notes.body:
Damping is the hardest property of a structure to predict, so it is usually measured. The course introduces three linked ways of describing it.

Damping factor ζ
- ζ = c/(2√(km)), the ratio of the actual damping coefficient to the critical value. Dimensionless.
- Typical values: lightly damped metal structures have ζ well under 0.05; adding damping treatment raises it.

Logarithmic decrement Λ
- For an underdamped free vibration, the ratio of successive peaks (one damped period apart) is constant: x_n/x_(n+1) = e^(ζωn × 2π/ωd).
- So Λ = ln(x_n/x_(n+1)) = 2πζ/√(1 − ζ²).
- For light damping, Λ ≈ 2πζ.
- Over N cycles: Λ = (1/N) ln(x₀/x_N). Using several cycles improves accuracy.
- Inverting exactly: ζ = Λ/√(4π² + Λ²).
- Worked example: amplitude falls from 10 mm to 2 mm in 5 cycles. Λ = (ln 5)/5 = 0.322, so ζ ≈ 0.322/(2π) ≈ 0.051.
- Worked example: successive peaks in the ratio 1.2 give Λ = ln 1.2 = 0.182 and ζ ≈ 0.029. If m = 5 kg and k = 2000 N/m, then c = 2ζ√(km) = 2 × 0.029 × 100 ≈ 5.8 N s/m.

Loss factor η
- η = (energy dissipated per cycle) / (2π × maximum strain energy stored).
- For a viscous dashpot at steady amplitude X and frequency ω: energy lost per cycle = πcωX², and maximum strain energy = ½kX², so η = cω/k = 2ζ(ω/ωn).
- At resonance (ω = ωn), η = 2ζ.
- For many materials the energy lost per cycle hardly depends on frequency. This is modelled as hysteretic damping with a complex stiffness k(1 + iη), where η is a material property.

Links to resonance
- The peak amplitude ratio at resonance for light damping is about 1/(2ζ), often called the quality factor Q.
- The half-power bandwidth (the frequency range over which the response exceeds 1/√2 of the peak) is approximately 2ζωn. So Q ≈ ωn/(bandwidth), and ζ can be measured from a forced test as well as a decay.
- Summary for light damping: Λ ≈ 2πζ, η (at resonance) = 2ζ, Q ≈ 1/(2ζ).

Exam tips: state whether you are using the exact or the light-damping formula, and use several cycles of a decay record rather than one.

notes.h: Two or more degrees of freedom: natural frequencies and mode shapes
notes.body:
Real structures need more than one coordinate. The number of degrees of freedom is the number of independent coordinates needed to describe the motion; for small vibrations it is also the number of natural frequencies.

Matrix equations of motion
- For masses linked by springs: M ẍ + K x = F, where x is the vector of displacements, M the mass matrix and K the stiffness matrix. Damping adds C ẋ.
- M is usually diagonal (one mass per coordinate). K is symmetric.
- Building K: the diagonal term Kᵢᵢ is the sum of stiffnesses of all springs attached to mass i; the off-diagonal term Kᵢⱼ is minus the stiffness of the spring directly joining masses i and j.
- Check: column j of K gives the forces needed on each mass when coordinate j is displaced by one unit and the others are held still (K is symmetric, so row j is the same).

Natural frequencies and mode shapes
- Look for free vibration in which all coordinates move harmonically in step: x = u cos ωt. Then (K − ω²M)u = 0.
- A non-zero u requires det(K − ω²M) = 0. This characteristic equation gives the natural frequencies (an eigenvalue problem).
- For each natural frequency, the corresponding vector u (eigenvector) is the mode shape: the fixed ratio of amplitudes in that mode. Its overall size is arbitrary.

Worked example 1: symmetric system
- Two equal masses m between two walls, joined wall–k–m–k–m–k–wall.
- K = k[[2, −1], [−1, 2]], M = mI.
- det: (2k − mω²)² − k² = 0, so 2k − mω² = ±k.
- ω₁ = √(k/m) with mode (1, 1): the masses move together and the middle spring is not stretched.
- ω₂ = √(3k/m) with mode (1, −1): the masses move in opposition.

Worked example 2: two-storey building model
- Ground–k–m–k–m (top free). K = [[2k, −k], [−k, k]].
- With λ = mω²/k: (2 − λ)(1 − λ) − 1 = λ² − 3λ + 1 = 0, so λ = (3 ∓ √5)/2 = 0.382 or 2.618.
- ω₁ = 0.618√(k/m) with mode (1, 1.618); ω₂ = 1.618√(k/m) with mode (1, −0.618).
- The lower mode has both floors moving the same way, with the top moving more; the higher mode has the floors moving in opposition.

Properties
- Lower modes generally have simpler shapes with fewer sign changes.
- The mode shapes are orthogonal with respect to the mass and stiffness matrices, which is what makes modal analysis work.

Exam tips: set up M and K carefully, expand the 2 × 2 determinant fully, and always give each mode shape as a ratio with a sketch.

notes.h: Free vibration by superposition of modes and harmonic excitation
notes.body:
Once the modes are known, any motion of a linear multi-degree-of-freedom system can be built from them.

Free vibration with initial conditions
- The general free response is a sum of modal motions: x(t) = Σ uᵢ (Aᵢ cos ωᵢt + Bᵢ sin ωᵢt).
- The Aᵢ are found by writing the initial displacement as a combination of mode shapes; the Bᵢ by writing the initial velocity as a combination and dividing each part by its ωᵢ.
- Example: the symmetric two-mass system (modes (1, 1) at ω₁ and (1, −1) at ω₂). Release from rest with x(0) = (a, 0). Since (a, 0) = (a/2)(1, 1) + (a/2)(1, −1):
- x₁ = (a/2)(cos ω₁t + cos ω₂t) and x₂ = (a/2)(cos ω₁t − cos ω₂t).
- If x(0) = (a, a) instead, only mode 1 is excited and the system vibrates purely at ω₁.

Beating and energy exchange
- If the middle (coupling) spring k_c is much softer than the outer springs k, the modes are close: ω₁ = √(k/m) and ω₂ = √((k + 2k_c)/m).
- Then x₁ = a cos(½(ω₂ − ω₁)t) cos(½(ω₁ + ω₂)t) and x₂ = a sin(½(ω₂ − ω₁)t) sin(½(ω₁ + ω₂)t).
- The vibration passes completely from mass 1 to mass 2 and back. Mass 1 is first still when t = π/(ω₂ − ω₁). These are beats.

Harmonic excitation
- With F = F₀ cos ωt applied, look for x = X cos ωt (undamped): (K − ω²M)X = F.
- Solve the 2 × 2 linear equations, for example by Cramer's rule. The determinant D(ω) = det(K − ω²M) appears in every denominator, so the response becomes infinite (undamped) at each natural frequency: there is one resonance per mode.
- Example: force F₀ on mass 1 of the symmetric system. D = (2k − mω²)² − k² = (k − mω²)(3k − mω²). Then X₁ = F₀(2k − mω²)/D and X₂ = F₀k/D.
- At ω² = 2k/m, X₁ = 0: the driven mass stands still (an antiresonance) while mass 2 moves with X₂ = −F₀/k, so the spring between them exactly balances the applied force. This idea underlies the vibration absorber.

Damping
- With damping, the amplitudes at each resonance are finite. For light damping each resonance looks like a single-degree-of-freedom resonance of its own mode.

Exam tips: decompose initial conditions into modes before writing the time response, check your answer at t = 0, and look for antiresonances when a question asks where the driven mass stays still.

The course ends with two practical uses of the theory: stopping vibration getting into or out of a machine, and cancelling it at a particular frequency.

Vibration isolation
- A machine (mass m) producing a harmonic force F₀ cos ωt sits on mounts of stiffness k and damping c. The force transmitted to the foundation is the spring force plus the damper force.
- Force transmissibility: |F_T|/F₀ = √(1 + (2ζr)²) / √((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²), with r = ω/ωn.
- The same expression gives the displacement transmissibility for a delicate instrument mounted on a vibrating base.
- Transmissibility equals 1 at r = √2 for all ζ. Isolation (transmissibility below 1) needs r > √2, i.e. a soft mount so that ωn is well below the forcing frequency.
- Damping limits the response when passing through resonance during start-up, but worsens isolation at high r.
- For light damping and r ≫ 1, transmissibility ≈ 1/(r² − 1).

Isolator design example
- A 100 kg machine runs at 3000 rpm (ω = 314 rad/s). Target transmissibility 0.1 with negligible damping.
- 1/(r² − 1) = 0.1 gives r² = 11, so ωn = 314/√11 ≈ 94.7 rad/s.
- k = mωn² ≈ 8.97 × 10⁵ N/m.
- Static deflection under the machine's weight = g/ωn² ≈ 1.09 mm. Designers often specify isolators by their static deflection.

Vibration absorbers
- A main system (M, K) is driven at a fixed frequency ω close to its resonance. Attach a small absorber mass m_a on a spring k_a.
- Equations of motion: Mẍ₁ + Kx₁ + k_a(x₁ − x₂) = F₀ cos ωt and m_a ẍ₂ + k_a(x₂ − x₁) = 0.
- Solving harmonically, X₁ = F₀(k_a − m_aω²)/D, where D is the system determinant.
- If the absorber is tuned so that √(k_a/m_a) = ω, then X₁ = 0: the main mass does not move. The absorber mass moves with X₂ = −F₀/k_a, so its spring pushes on the main mass with a force that cancels F₀ at every instant.
- Limitations: it only works near one frequency; the coupled system now has two resonances, one either side of the tuned frequency, so running speed must not drift; the absorber spring must be designed for the motion F₀/k_a.
- Adding damping to the absorber widens the useful frequency band at the cost of perfect cancellation.

Exam tips: for isolation, always check whether you are above √2; for absorbers, write the two equations of motion, solve for X₁, and state the tuning condition clearly.

questions.q: In the force–voltage analogy between a mass–spring–dashpot system and a series LCR circuit, which element corresponds to the spring?
questions.why: Comparing mẍ + cẋ + kx = F with Lq̈ + Rq̇ + q/C = V, stiffness k corresponds to 1/C, so the spring is the capacitor (compliance ↔ capacitance). The inductor matches the mass, the resistor the dashpot, and the voltage source the applied force.

questions.q: Springs of stiffness 2k and 3k are connected in series. What is the equivalent stiffness?
questions.why: In series, 1/k_eq = 1/(2k) + 1/(3k) = 5/(6k), so k_eq = 6k/5 = 1.2k. 5k is the parallel result; 6k is the product rule without dividing by the sum; 0.83k is 5/6, the reciprocal slip.

questions.q: A mass m sits on a smooth floor between two walls. It is joined to the left wall by a spring k₁ and to the right wall by a spring k₂ in parallel with a dashpot c. A horizontal force F(t) acts on the mass. Derive its equation of motion, give expressions for ωn and ζ, and state the electrical analogue.
markScheme: Displace m by x to the right: spring k₁ stretches and pulls left with k₁x; spring k₂ compresses and pushes left with k₂x; dashpot force cẋ to the left
mẍ = F − (k₁ + k₂)x − cẋ, i.e. mẍ + cẋ + (k₁ + k₂)x = F
ωn = √((k₁ + k₂)/m)
Analogue: series LCR circuit with L ↔ m, R ↔ c, 1/C ↔ k₁ + k₂, V ↔ F
questions.modelAnswer: Measure x from the equilibrium position, positive to the right. When the mass moves right by x, spring k₁ is stretched by x and pulls the mass left with force k₁x; spring k₂ is compressed by x and pushes left with k₂x; the dashpot resists the velocity with force cẋ to the left. Newton's second law: mẍ = F − k₁x − k₂x − cẋ, so mẍ + cẋ + (k₁ + k₂)x = F. The springs act in parallel on the mass, so ωn = √((k₁ + k₂)/m) and ζ = c/(2√((k₁ + k₂)m)). The electrical analogue is a series LCR circuit driven by a voltage source: L corresponds to m, R to c, 1/C to k₁ + k₂, charge to x and voltage to F.

questions.q: A spring of stiffness 1000 N/m in parallel with a dashpot of 50 N s/m is suddenly loaded by a constant force. Roughly how long does the displacement take to reach 95% of its final value?
questions.why: T = c/k = 0.05 s, and 1 − e^(−t/T) = 0.95 gives t = T ln 20 ≈ 3T = 0.15 s. 0.05 s is one time constant (63%); 0.10 s is 2T (86%); 0.25 s is 5T (99.3%).

questions.q: A first-order system with time constant T is driven by a unit ramp input. Once the transient has died away, how does the output compare with the input?
options: It grows exponentially away from the input
It levels off at a constant value T
It has the same slope but lags the input by T
questions.why: y = t − T + Te^(−t/T) → t − T, so the output runs parallel to the ramp, lagging by T. It does not follow exactly (the lag remains), it does not diverge, and it does not level off because the input keeps rising.

questions.q: A first-order system has time constant T = 0.2 s. (a) For a unit step input, find the output at t = 0.2 s and the time to reach 90% of the final value. (b) Write down its unit impulse response and explain how it relates to the step response.
markScheme: Step response y = 1 − e^(−t/T)
Impulse response y = (1/T)e^(−t/T) = 5e^(−5t)
It is the time derivative of the step response, because a unit impulse is the derivative of a unit step and the system is linear
questions.modelAnswer: (a) For Tẏ + y = x with a unit step and y(0) = 0, the response is y = 1 − e^(−t/T). At t = 0.2 s = T, y = 1 − e⁻¹ ≈ 0.632. For 90%, e^(−t/T) = 0.1, so t = T ln 10 = 0.2 × 2.303 ≈ 0.46 s. (b) The unit impulse response is y = (1/T)e^(−t/T) = 5e^(−5t). A unit impulse is the time derivative of a unit step, and for a linear time-invariant system the response to the derivative of an input is the derivative of the response, so the impulse response is d/dt(1 − e^(−t/T)) = (1/T)e^(−t/T).

questions.q: A first-order system with T = 0.01 s is driven sinusoidally at ω = 200 rad/s. What are the amplitude ratio and phase lag of the steady response?
questions.why: ωT = 2, so the ratio is 1/√(1 + 4) = 0.447 and the lag is arctan 2 = 63.4°. 0.707 and 45° apply at ωT = 1; 0.5 is the high-frequency approximation 1/(ωT), which is not accurate at ωT = 2, and 60° does not follow from arctan(ωT); 0.894 and 26.6° correspond to ωT = 0.5.

questions.q: When using x = Re(Xe^(iωt)) to find a steady harmonic response, what does the second derivative ẍ become?
questions.why: Each differentiation multiplies by iω, so two give (iω)² = −ω². ω² misses the sign from i²; iω is a single derivative; −iω corresponds to e^(−iωt).

questions.q: Using complex exponentials, find the steady-state response of Tẏ + y = X cos ωt. Give the amplitude and phase of y, and describe the behaviour at low frequency, at ω = 1/T and at high frequency.
markScheme: Writes input as Re(Xe^(iωt)) and tries y = Re(Ye^(iωt))
(1 + iωT)Y = X, so Y/X = 1/(1 + iωT)
Amplitude X/√(1 + ω²T²), phase lag arctan(ωT): y = (X/√(1 + ω²T²)) cos(ωt − arctan ωT)
Low frequency: ratio → 1, lag → 0; at ω = 1/T: ratio 1/√2, lag 45°
High frequency: ratio ≈ 1/(ωT), lag → 90°
questions.modelAnswer: Write the input as Re(Xe^(iωt)) and look for y = Re(Ye^(iωt)). Substituting, iωT Y + Y = X, so Y/X = 1/(1 + iωT). The modulus is 1/√(1 + ω²T²) and the argument is −arctan(ωT). So y = (X/√(1 + ω²T²)) cos(ωt − φ) with φ = arctan(ωT), a phase lag. At low frequency (ωT ≪ 1) the output follows the input with ratio near 1 and almost no lag. At ω = 1/T the ratio is 1/√2 (−3 dB) and the lag is 45°. At high frequency (ωT ≫ 1) the ratio is approximately 1/(ωT), so it falls tenfold for every tenfold rise in frequency, and the lag tends to 90°.

questions.q: A system has m = 2 kg, k = 800 N/m and c = 8 N s/m. What are ωn and ζ?
questions.why: ωn = √(800/2) = 20 rad/s and ζ = c/(2√(km)) = 8/(2 × 40) = 0.1. 0.2 forgets the factor 2 in c_c; 400 is ωn²; 3.18 is fn in Hz, not rad/s.

questions.q: A system is released from a displaced position and returns to equilibrium as fast as possible without overshooting. Which damping condition is this?
questions.why: Critical damping (ζ = 1) gives the fastest non-oscillatory return. Underdamped systems overshoot and oscillate; overdamped systems do not overshoot but return more slowly; undamped systems oscillate forever.

questions.q: An underdamped system (natural frequency ωn, damping factor ζ < 1) is released from rest with displacement x₀. Derive its free response and state the time constant of the decay envelope.
markScheme: Characteristic roots λ = −ζωn ± iωd with ωd = ωn√(1 − ζ²)
General solution x = e^(−ζωn t)(A cos ωd t + B sin ωd t)
x(0) = x₀ gives A = x₀
ẋ(0) = 0 gives −ζωn A + ωd B = 0, so B = ζωn x₀/ωd = x₀ζ/√(1 − ζ²)
Envelope ∝ e^(−ζωn t), time constant 1/(ζωn)
questions.modelAnswer: With mẍ + cẋ + kx = 0, try x = e^(λt): λ² + 2ζωnλ + ωn² = 0, so λ = −ζωn ± iωn√(1 − ζ²) = −ζωn ± iωd. The real solution is x = e^(−ζωn t)(A cos ωd t + B sin ωd t). At t = 0, x = x₀ gives A = x₀. Differentiating, ẋ(0) = −ζωn A + ωd B = 0, so B = ζωn x₀/ωd = x₀ζ/√(1 − ζ²). Hence x = x₀e^(−ζωn t)[cos ωd t + (ζ/√(1 − ζ²)) sin ωd t]. The oscillation sits inside an envelope proportional to e^(−ζωn t), which has time constant 1/(ζωn).

questions.q: A second-order system with ζ = 0.1 is subjected to a suddenly applied constant force. By roughly how much does its peak displacement exceed the static deflection?
questions.why: Overshoot = exp(−πζ/√(1 − ζ²)) = exp(−0.316) ≈ 0.73. 100% is the undamped case; 10% simply repeats ζ; 27% is 1 − 0.73.

questions.q: An undamped mass–spring system (m = 2 kg, k = 800 N/m) at rest is struck by an impulse of 4 N s. What is the amplitude of the resulting vibration?
questions.why: The impulse gives v₀ = I/m = 2 m/s with x = 0, so x = (v₀/ωn) sin ωn t with ωn = 20 rad/s, giving amplitude 0.1 m. 0.2 m is I/ωn, forgetting to divide the impulse by the mass to get the velocity; 0.005 m is I/k; 2 m is the initial velocity value.

questions.q: Show that when a constant force F₀ is suddenly applied to an undamped mass–spring system at rest, the maximum displacement is twice the static deflection. Explain briefly why this matters in design.
markScheme: Equation mẍ + kx = F₀; particular integral F₀/k
General solution x = F₀/k + A cos ωn t + B sin ωn t
x(0) = 0 and ẋ(0) = 0 give A = −F₀/k, B = 0, so x = (F₀/k)(1 − cos ωn t)
Maximum when cos ωn t = −1: x_max = 2F₀/k; a suddenly applied load can cause twice the static stress
questions.modelAnswer: The equation of motion is mẍ + kx = F₀ for t ≥ 0. A particular integral is the static deflection F₀/k, so x = F₀/k + A cos ωn t + B sin ωn t. At t = 0 the mass is at rest at x = 0: x(0) = 0 gives A = −F₀/k and ẋ(0) = 0 gives B = 0. So x = (F₀/k)(1 − cos ωn t), which oscillates between 0 and 2F₀/k. The peak is twice the static deflection. In design, a load that is applied suddenly (for example a dropped weight just touching a structure, or a valve slamming shut) can produce up to twice the deflection and stress of the same load applied slowly, so a dynamic factor must be allowed for.

questions.q: A system with m = 2 kg, k = 800 N/m and ζ = 0.1 is driven by a 10 N harmonic force at 40 rad/s. What is the steady displacement amplitude?
questions.why: ωn = 20 rad/s, so r = 2. |X| = (F₀/k)/√((1 − 4)² + (0.4)²) = 12.5/3.03 ≈ 4.13 mm. 62.5 mm is the resonant amplitude; 12.5 mm is the static deflection; 3.1 mm is the mass-controlled approximation F₀/(mω²), which is not accurate this close to resonance.

questions.q: At resonance (ω = ωn), what is the phase of the displacement of a damped single-degree-of-freedom system relative to the applied force?
questions.why: At r = 1, tan φ = 2ζ/0 → ∞, so φ = 90° lag; the velocity is then in phase with the force. In phase applies at low frequency; 180° lag is approached at high frequency; displacement never leads the force in this system.

questions.q: A system has m = 2 kg, k = 800 N/m and c = 8 N s/m and is driven by a harmonic force of amplitude 10 N. Find the static deflection, the amplitude at resonance, and describe how the amplitude and phase behave well below and well above resonance.
markScheme: ωn = 20 rad/s, ζ = 0.1
Static deflection F₀/k = 12.5 mm
Resonant amplitude (F₀/k)/(2ζ) = 62.5 mm, lagging the force by 90°
Well below resonance: |X| ≈ F₀/k, in phase (stiffness-controlled)
Well above resonance: |X| ≈ F₀/(mω²), falling as 1/ω², nearly 180° out of phase (mass-controlled)
questions.modelAnswer: ωn = √(800/2) = 20 rad/s and ζ = 8/(2√(800 × 2)) = 0.1. The static deflection is F₀/k = 10/800 = 12.5 mm. At resonance the amplitude ratio is 1/(2ζ) = 5, so the amplitude is 62.5 mm, lagging the force by 90°; only the dashpot limits it. Well below resonance (r ≪ 1) the spring dominates: the amplitude is close to 12.5 mm and in phase with the force. Well above resonance (r ≫ 1) the mass dominates: the amplitude is approximately F₀/(mω²), falling as 1/ω², and the displacement is nearly 180° out of phase with the force.

questions.q: The amplitude of a free vibration falls from 10 mm to 2 mm over 5 cycles. What is the approximate damping factor?
questions.why: Λ = (1/5) ln(10/2) = 0.322 per cycle, and ζ ≈ Λ/(2π) ≈ 0.051. 0.322 is Λ itself; 0.256 is ln 5/(2π), forgetting to divide by 5 cycles; 0.102 is Λ/π, missing a factor of 2.

questions.q: For a lightly damped system with viscous damping, what is the loss factor η at resonance?
questions.why: η = cω/k = 2ζω/ωn, which equals 2ζ at ω = ωn. ζ alone misses the factor 2; 2πζ is the (approximate) logarithmic decrement; 1/(2ζ) is the quality factor Q.

questions.q: A free-vibration test on a system with m = 5 kg and k = 2000 N/m shows successive peaks in the ratio 1.2. Find the logarithmic decrement, the damping factor and the damping coefficient c.
markScheme: ζ = Λ/√(4π² + Λ²) ≈ 0.029 (light-damping formula Λ/2π gives the same to 3 s.f.)
Comments that ζ is small, so ωd ≈ ωn = 20 rad/s
questions.modelAnswer: The logarithmic decrement is Λ = ln(x_n/x_(n+1)) = ln 1.2 = 0.182. The exact relation gives ζ = Λ/√(4π² + Λ²) = 0.182/√(39.48 + 0.033) ≈ 0.0290; the light-damping approximation Λ/(2π) gives 0.0290 as well. Then √(km) = √(2000 × 5) = 100 kg/s, so c = 2ζ√(km) ≈ 2 × 0.0290 × 100 ≈ 5.8 N s/m. The damping is light, so the damped natural frequency is essentially ωn = √(2000/5) = 20 rad/s.

questions.q: Two equal masses m are connected in a line between two fixed walls by three identical springs k (wall–k–m–k–m–k–wall). What are the natural frequencies?
questions.why: det([[2k − mω², −k], [−k, 2k − mω²]]) = 0 gives 2k − mω² = ±k, so ω² = k/m (in-phase mode, middle spring unstretched) or 3k/m (anti-phase mode). The other options come from mistakes in the diagonal stiffness terms.

questions.q: What is a mode shape?
options: The shape of the amplitude–frequency curve near resonance
The static deflected shape under self-weight
The set of all natural frequencies of the system
The fixed ratio of amplitudes of the coordinates when the system vibrates freely at one natural frequency
questions.why: A mode shape is the eigenvector of (K − ω²M)u = 0 at a natural frequency: the pattern of relative amplitudes. The resonance curve, static deflection and list of frequencies are different things.

questions.q: A two-storey building is modelled as two floors, each of mass m, with the lower floor joined to the ground by a storey stiffness k and the upper floor joined to the lower by another k. Set up M and K, and find the natural frequencies and mode shapes.
markScheme: Equations: mẍ₁ + 2kx₁ − kx₂ = 0 and mẍ₂ − kx₁ + kx₂ = 0; M = mI, K = [[2k, −k], [−k, k]]
det(K − ω²M) = 0 with λ = mω²/k gives λ² − 3λ + 1 = 0
Mode shapes from second row x₂/x₁ = k/(k − mω²) = 1/(1 − λ)
Mode 1: (1, 1.618), both floors same direction; mode 2: (1, −0.618), floors in opposition
questions.modelAnswer: Let x₁ and x₂ be the floor displacements. The lower floor feels −kx₁ from the ground spring and −k(x₁ − x₂) from the upper spring, so mẍ₁ + 2kx₁ − kx₂ = 0. The upper floor feels −k(x₂ − x₁), so mẍ₂ − kx₁ + kx₂ = 0. Hence M = mI and K = [[2k, −k], [−k, k]]. Setting det(K − ω²M) = 0 with λ = mω²/k: (2 − λ)(1 − λ) − 1 = λ² − 3λ + 1 = 0, so λ = (3 ∓ √5)/2 = 0.382 or 2.618. Thus ω₁ = √0.382 √(k/m) = 0.618√(k/m) and ω₂ = √2.618 √(k/m) = 1.618√(k/m). From the second row, x₂/x₁ = k/(k − mω²) = 1/(1 − λ). Mode 1: 1/(1 − 0.382) = 1.618, so (1, 1.618): both floors move the same way, the top floor more. Mode 2: 1/(1 − 2.618) = −0.618, so (1, −0.618): the floors move in opposite directions.

questions.q: Two equal masses on three equal springs between walls (modes (1, 1) and (1, −1)) are released from rest with x₁ = a and x₂ = 0. What are the amplitudes of the two modes?
questions.why: (a, 0) = (a/2)(1, 1) + (a/2)(1, −1), so each mode has amplitude a/2. Exciting mode 1 alone needs (a, a); mode 2 alone needs (a, −a); amplitude a in each would give initial displacement (2a, 0).

questions.q: For the symmetric system wall–k–m–k–m–k–wall, a harmonic force acts on mass 1 only. At what frequency does mass 1 stay still?
questions.why: X₁ = F₀(2k − mω²)/D, which is zero when ω² = 2k/m: an antiresonance. Mass 2 then moves with X₂ = −F₀/k so the spring between them cancels the force. √(k/m) and √(3k/m) are the resonances, where the undamped response is infinite.

questions.q: For two equal masses m on three equal springs k between walls (natural frequencies ω₁ = √(k/m), ω₂ = √(3k/m)), both masses start at their equilibrium positions. Mass 1 is given velocity u and mass 2 is at rest. Find x₁(t) and x₂(t) by modal superposition.
markScheme: Modes (1, 1) at ω₁ and (1, −1) at ω₂; zero initial displacement so only sine terms
Decompose initial velocity: (u, 0) = (u/2)(1, 1) + (u/2)(1, −1)
Each modal velocity amplitude divided by its frequency: x = (u/2ω₁)(1, 1) sin ω₁t + (u/2ω₂)(1, −1) sin ω₂t
x₁ = (u/2)(sin ω₁t/ω₁ + sin ω₂t/ω₂)
x₂ = (u/2)(sin ω₁t/ω₁ − sin ω₂t/ω₂); check ẋ(0) = (u, 0)
questions.modelAnswer: The modes are (1, 1) at ω₁ = √(k/m) and (1, −1) at ω₂ = √(3k/m). The general free response is x = (1, 1)(A₁ cos ω₁t + B₁ sin ω₁t) + (1, −1)(A₂ cos ω₂t + B₂ sin ω₂t). Zero initial displacement gives A₁ = A₂ = 0. The initial velocity (u, 0) splits as (u/2)(1, 1) + (u/2)(1, −1), so B₁ω₁ = u/2 and B₂ω₂ = u/2. Therefore x₁ = (u/2)(sin ω₁t/ω₁ + sin ω₂t/ω₂) and x₂ = (u/2)(sin ω₁t/ω₁ − sin ω₂t/ω₂). Check: at t = 0 both are zero, and ẋ₁(0) = (u/2)(1 + 1) = u, ẋ₂(0) = (u/2)(1 − 1) = 0, as required.

questions.q: For a machine on spring mounts, above what frequency ratio r = ω/ωn does the mounting start to reduce the force transmitted to the floor?
questions.why: Transmissibility equals 1 at r = √2 for every damping level and is below 1 only for r > √2. At r = 1 the mount amplifies the force (resonance); r = 2 is already well into the isolation region; 1/√2 is below resonance.

questions.q: A machine is driven at a fixed frequency ω close to its resonance. An undamped absorber (mass m_a, spring k_a) is attached. What tuning makes the machine stand still?
options: k_a = k of the machine mounts
questions.why: With √(k_a/m_a) = ω, the factor (k_a − m_aω²) in the numerator of X₁ vanishes, so the main mass does not move; the absorber spring force cancels the applied force. The other choices do not make that factor zero.

questions.q: A 100 kg machine runs at 3000 rpm and is to be mounted on undamped springs so that only 10% of its unbalanced force reaches the floor. Find the required total mount stiffness and the static deflection of the mounts. Comment on what happens during start-up.
markScheme: For undamped mounts with r > √2, transmissibility = 1/(r² − 1) = 0.1 so r² = 11
k = mωn² ≈ 8.97 × 10⁵ N/m (about 0.9 MN/m)
Static deflection g/ωn² ≈ 1.09 mm; machine passes through resonance during start-up, so some damping or a fast run-up is needed
questions.modelAnswer: The running speed is ω = 3000 × 2π/60 ≈ 314.2 rad/s. With negligible damping and r > √2, the transmissibility is 1/(r² − 1). Setting this equal to 0.1 gives r² − 1 = 10, so r² = 11 and ωn = 314.2/√11 ≈ 94.7 rad/s. The total mount stiffness is k = mωn² = 100 × 94.7² ≈ 8.97 × 10⁵ N/m. The static deflection under the machine's weight is mg/k = g/ωn² = 9.81/8972 ≈ 1.09 mm. During start-up the forcing frequency rises through ωn ≈ 94.7 rad/s (about 905 rpm), where undamped mounts would allow very large motion and transmitted force, so some damping should be added or the machine run up quickly through that speed, accepting slightly worse isolation at the running speed.

questions.q:
A 200 kg machine is mounted on springs of total stiffness 8 × 10⁵ N/m with some damping. A free-vibration test shows that successive peaks are in the ratio 1.5.
(a) Find the undamped natural frequency (in rad/s and Hz), the damping factor and the damping coefficient. [6]
(b) In service the machine runs at 1200 rpm and its rotating unbalance produces a harmonic force of amplitude 500 N at this speed. Find the steady displacement amplitude and the amplitude of the force transmitted to the floor. [8]
(c) The unbalance force is proportional to the square of the speed. Estimate the displacement amplitude and transmitted force amplitude as the machine passes slowly through resonance during start-up, and comment. [6]
markScheme: (b) Transmissibility √(1 + (2ζr)²)/2.96 ≈ 0.35; transmitted force ≈ 174 N
(c) At resonance force amplitude = 500 × (63.2/125.7)² ≈ 127 N; |X| = (F/k)/(2ζ) ≈ 1.2 mm
(c) Transmitted force ≈ F × √(1 + 4ζ²)/(2ζ) ≈ 127 × 7.8 ≈ 990 N, much more than at running speed; comment on fast run-up or more damping, and on the trade-off with isolation at running speed
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) ωn = √(k/m) = √(8 × 10⁵/200) = √4000 ≈ 63.2 rad/s, i.e. fn = 63.2/(2π) ≈ 10.1 Hz. The logarithmic decrement is Λ = ln 1.5 ≈ 0.405. Then ζ = Λ/√(4π² + Λ²) = 0.405/√(39.48 + 0.164) ≈ 0.064 (the light-damping formula Λ/2π gives 0.065). √(km) = √(8 × 10⁵ × 200) = √(1.6 × 10⁸) ≈ 12,650 kg/s, so c = 2ζ√(km) ≈ 2 × 0.0644 × 12,650 ≈ 1630 N s/m.

(b) The running speed is ω = 1200 × 2π/60 ≈ 125.7 rad/s, so r = 125.7/63.2 ≈ 1.99. The static deflection under 500 N is F₀/k = 500/(8 × 10⁵) = 6.25 × 10⁻⁴ m. The denominator is √((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²) = √((1 − 3.948)² + (0.256)²) = √(8.69 + 0.066) ≈ 2.96. So |X| ≈ 6.25 × 10⁻⁴/2.96 ≈ 2.1 × 10⁻⁴ m = 0.21 mm. The force transmitted through the springs and dashpot has transmissibility √(1 + (2ζr)²)/2.96 = √1.066/2.96 ≈ 1.032/2.96 ≈ 0.35, so the transmitted force amplitude is about 0.35 × 500 ≈ 174 N. The mounts are working as isolators because r ≈ 2 > √2.

(c) At resonance the speed is ωn ≈ 63.2 rad/s. The unbalance force scales with speed squared, so its amplitude there is 500 × (63.2/125.7)² ≈ 500 × 0.253 ≈ 127 N. At r = 1 the amplitude is (F/k)/(2ζ) = (127/8 × 10⁵)/(0.129) ≈ 1.58 × 10⁻⁴/0.129 ≈ 1.2 × 10⁻³ m, about 1.2 mm, roughly six times the running amplitude. The transmissibility at r = 1 is √(1 + (2ζ)²)/(2ζ) ≈ 1.008/0.129 ≈ 7.8, so the transmitted force is about 127 × 7.8 ≈ 990 N, nearly six times the force transmitted at running speed even though the applied force is only a quarter as large. In practice the machine passes through resonance quickly, so steady-state values are an upper estimate; nevertheless the result shows why some damping is useful in isolators. More damping would reduce these resonant peaks but would increase the force transmitted at the running speed (r > √2), so the designer must balance the two.

questions.q:
Two identical pendulum-like oscillators are modelled as two masses m = 1 kg on a smooth surface, each joined to a fixed wall by a spring k = 100 N/m and joined to each other by a weak coupling spring k_c = 5 N/m (wall–k–m–k_c–m–k–wall).
(a) Write the equations of motion in matrix form. [3]
(b) Find the natural frequencies and mode shapes. [6]
(c) Mass 1 is held at x₁ = a with mass 2 at x₂ = 0, and both are released from rest. Find x₁(t) and x₂(t). [5]
(d) Show that the motion can be written as a product of a fast and a slow oscillation, and find the time at which mass 1 first comes completely to rest while mass 2 has its full amplitude. [6]
markScheme: (a) mẍ₁ + (k + k_c)x₁ − k_c x₂ = 0; mẍ₂ − k_c x₁ + (k + k_c)x₂ = 0; M = mI, K = [[k + k_c, −k_c], [−k_c, k + k_c]]
(b) det: (k + k_c − mω²)² = k_c², so mω² = k or k + 2k_c
(c) (a, 0) = (a/2)(1, 1) + (a/2)(1, −1); zero initial velocity so cosines only
(c) x₁ = (a/2)(cos ω₁t + cos ω₂t), x₂ = (a/2)(cos ω₁t − cos ω₂t)
(d) Sum-to-product: x₁ = a cos(½(ω₂ − ω₁)t) cos(½(ω₁ + ω₂)t); x₂ = a sin(½(ω₂ − ω₁)t) sin(½(ω₁ + ω₂)t)
(d) Fast frequency ≈ 10.24 rad/s inside slow envelope with ½(ω₂ − ω₁) ≈ 0.244 rad/s
(d) Mass 1 first at rest (envelope zero) when ½(ω₂ − ω₁)t = π/2, t = π/(ω₂ − ω₁) ≈ π/0.488 ≈ 6.4 s
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Let x₁ and x₂ be measured from equilibrium. Mass 1 feels −kx₁ from its wall spring and −k_c(x₁ − x₂) from the coupling spring: mẍ₁ + (k + k_c)x₁ − k_c x₂ = 0. Similarly mẍ₂ − k_c x₁ + (k + k_c)x₂ = 0. In matrix form M ẍ + K x = 0 with M = mI and K = [[k + k_c, −k_c], [−k_c, k + k_c]].

(b) Setting det(K − ω²M) = 0: (k + k_c − mω²)² − k_c² = 0, so k + k_c − mω² = ±k_c. Taking +k_c gives mω² = k, so ω₁ = √(k/m) = √100 = 10 rad/s; substituting into the first row, (k_c)u₁ − k_c u₂ = 0, so the mode is (1, 1): the masses move together and the coupling spring is not stretched. Taking −k_c gives mω² = k + 2k_c, so ω₂ = √(110) ≈ 10.488 rad/s, with mode (1, −1): the masses move in opposition, stretching the coupling spring.

(c) The general free response is x = (1, 1)(A₁ cos ω₁t + B₁ sin ω₁t) + (1, −1)(A₂ cos ω₂t + B₂ sin ω₂t). Released from rest, so B₁ = B₂ = 0. The initial displacement (a, 0) = (a/2)(1, 1) + (a/2)(1, −1), so A₁ = A₂ = a/2. Hence x₁ = (a/2)(cos ω₁t + cos ω₂t) and x₂ = (a/2)(cos ω₁t − cos ω₂t).

(d) Using cos A + cos B = 2 cos((A + B)/2) cos((A − B)/2) and cos A − cos B = 2 sin((A + B)/2) sin((B − A)/2): x₁ = a cos(½(ω₂ − ω₁)t) cos(½(ω₁ + ω₂)t) and x₂ = a sin(½(ω₂ − ω₁)t) sin(½(ω₁ + ω₂)t). Each mass vibrates at the fast mean frequency ½(ω₁ + ω₂) ≈ 10.24 rad/s, inside a slowly varying envelope at ½(ω₂ − ω₁) ≈ 0.244 rad/s. The envelopes of x₁ and x₂ are a cos and a sin of the same slow angle, so vibration energy passes back and forth between the masses (beats). Mass 1's envelope first reaches zero when ½(ω₂ − ω₁)t = π/2, i.e. t = π/(ω₂ − ω₁) = π/0.488 ≈ 6.4 s. At that moment mass 2's envelope equals a: all the vibration has transferred to mass 2. The weaker the coupling, the closer ω₁ and ω₂ and the slower this exchange.
